lines.text: Nearly all of us keep a small museum that no one else would want to visit.
A concert ticket. A pebble from one particular beach. The key to a flat we left long ago.
To anyone else, they are clutter. To us, they are proof that a certain afternoon really happened.
Memory is a poor archivist. It fades, it edits, it flatters.
A stone in the hand cannot be argued with.
And so we grip these things a little too tightly.
We fear that if the object goes, the person or the summer goes with it.
The drawers fill up, and the past becomes something we carry rather than visit.
Yet the object was never the memory. It was only a door.
What happened lives on in us: in how we laugh, what we notice, who we become.
Keep the few things that still open something.
And let the rest go, gently, with thanks.
